newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP concerned at Asian oil benchmark.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP concerned at Asian oil benchmark.

text.p: Australian oil producer and explorer The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said on Monday it would be keen to support the development of an alternative to Tapis as an industry benchmark for Asian oil.

The Tapis price quoted by the Asian Petroleum Price Index (APPI) was becoming less and less indicative of the price at which light sweet Asian oil grades had been sold, said BHP Petroleum crude oil marketing manager, strategy and risk management, Chris Gascoyne.
Any seller who had recently linked term prices to APPI would have incurred a significant opportunity loss, Gascoyne told the Asia-Pacific Commodity Markets Conference.
He said BHP no longer linked all its contracts to the benchmark. "If they had been, over the last six or 12 months, we would have lost many, many millions of dollars," he said.
The Tapis price quoted by the APPI was based on prices from a panel of producers, refiners and traders, he said.
However, during the past six months Tapis had traded on the spot market at US$0.50-US$1.00 a barrel above the APPI quotation, and up to US$1.50 recently.
Gasgoyne said one reason for the distortion was the declining amount of Tapis on the market due to increased consumption in Malaysia.
Although about 330,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Tapis was produced, only 50,000-70,000 bpd was sold on the export market.
At the same time, some producers on the APPI panel appeared to be putting in a price below the fair market price, he said.
"Part of the problem is that a number of producers ... reward their marketing people and set their benchmarks and taxation arrangements on APPI quotations," he said.
Gascoyne said market manipulation was also a risk given that up to 1.5 million bpd was priced directly or indirectly off Tapis, in spite of its small export volume.

One solution was to price the Asian market off Brent oil. However, Brent prices could often move on local events and Asian refiners would not be happy paying higher prices "based on a storm in the North Sea", he said.
An alternative would be to create an "Asian basket", based on Australian, Papua New Guinean, Malaysian and Atlantic Basin production, he said.
Indonesia already had a pricing formula which included Tapis, Gippsland, Arun, Minas and Dubai, although this would need to be modified to make it more market responsive.
Gascoyne said NYMEX and the Sydney Futures Exchange were investigating the potential for a formula of this type, but were at least a year away from any result.
